Adding Rule-Based Named Entities

Kenneth Benoit

2026-11-10

Source: vignettes/articles/entity_rules.Rmd
entity_rules.Rmd

Introduction

spaCy’s language models recognise named entities statistically, from what they learned in training. They often miss entities that matter for a particular study: names specific to a field, organisations the model has never seen, or entities that the model’s training data marked differently from how a researcher would. A common example (#234) is people’s academic titles, which spaCy’s English models leave out of a PERSON entity.

spaCy solves this with an entity ruler, a pipeline component that adds entities by matching rules: phrases, or sequences of tokens described by their attributes. spacyr lets you create these rules in R, and adds them to the pipeline when it initializes spaCy:

  • as_entity_patterns() creates a set of rules from phrases, spaCy’s own pattern structure, a data.frame, a quanteda dictionary, or entities that spaCy has already found;
  • entity_patterns_read() and entity_patterns_write() read and write rules as files, in spaCy’s JSONL format;
  • spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = ) adds the rules to the pipeline.

Creating rules needs neither Python nor spaCy, so the rules are ordinary R objects that can be inspected, combined and saved.

If spaCy is already running in your R session, call spacy_finalize() before calling spacy_initialize() with a new set of rules.

library("spacyr")

Phrases

The simplest rule is a phrase with a label. The names of a character vector give the labels:

pats <- as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "Acme Widgets", GPE = "Ruritania"))
pats
## Entity patterns: 2 patterns (ORG: 1, GPE: 1)
##   ORG  "Acme Widgets"
##   GPE  "Ruritania"

Without rules, the model finds some of these entities, but not as we would label them:

txt <- "Acme Widgets opened a factory in Ruritania, said Jane Smith."
spacy_initialize()
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id         text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Acme Widgets   PERSON        1      2
## 2  text1    Ruritania      GPE        7      1
## 3  text1   Jane Smith   PERSON       10      2
spacy_finalize()

With the rules, it finds both, with our labels, and still finds the entities that the rules say nothing about:

spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = pats)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id         text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Acme Widgets      ORG        1      2
## 2  text1    Ruritania      GPE        7      1
## 3  text1   Jane Smith   PERSON       10      2
spacy_parse(txt, pos = FALSE, lemma = FALSE)
##    doc_id sentence_id token_id     token   entity
## 1   text1           1        1      Acme    ORG_B
## 2   text1           1        2   Widgets    ORG_I
## 3   text1           1        3    opened         
## 4   text1           1        4         a         
## 5   text1           1        5   factory         
## 6   text1           1        6        in         
## 7   text1           1        7 Ruritania    GPE_B
## 8   text1           1        8         ,         
## 9   text1           1        9      said         
## 10  text1           1       10      Jane PERSON_B
## 11  text1           1       11     Smith PERSON_I
## 12  text1           1       12         .
spacy_finalize()

Phrases match spaCy’s tokens exactly, including their case. With case_insensitive = TRUE, they match in any case:

pats <- as_entity_patterns(c("Acme Widgets", "Globex"), label = "ORG",
                           case_insensitive = TRUE)
pats
## Entity patterns: 2 patterns (ORG: 2)
##   ORG  "Acme Widgets" (any case)
##   ORG  "Globex" (any case)
spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = pats)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity("ACME WIDGETS and globex announced a merger.")
##   doc_id         text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 ACME WIDGETS      ORG        1      2
## 2  text1       globex      ORG        4      1
spacy_finalize()

A phrase is split into tokens by the pipeline’s own tokenizer, so "Globex, Inc." is matched as the three tokens Globex, , and Inc., as in a text. Some rules of the tokenizer depend on case, though: spaCy’s English models keep "Inc." as one token, but split "inc." into "inc" and ".". So write phrases in their usual case, even when they should match in any case.

Token patterns

Rules can also describe a sequence of tokens by their attributes, in spaCy’s own structure: a list with one element per token, each a named list of attributes such as LOWER (the token in lower case), IS_TITLE, ENT_TYPE (the type of entity a token belongs to) or OP (how many times the token may occur).

To include academic titles in PERSON entities, we match a title, followed by the tokens of a person that the model has already recognised:

titles <- c("dr", "dr.", "prof", "prof.", "professor")
title_rule <- as_entity_patterns(list(
  label = "PERSON",
  pattern = list(list(LOWER = list(IN = titles)),
                 list(ENT_TYPE = "PERSON", ENT_IOB = "B"),
                 list(ENT_TYPE = "PERSON", ENT_IOB = "I", OP = "*"))
))
title_rule
## Entity patterns: 1 pattern (PERSON: 1)
##   PERSON  [LOWER in (dr, dr., prof, prof., professor)] [ENT_TYPE = PERSON, ENT_IOB = B] [ENT_TYPE = PERSON, ENT_IOB = I]*

The second token begins a PERSON entity (ENT_IOB = "B"), and the third matches the rest of that entity (ENT_IOB = "I"), zero or more times. A simpler rule, a title followed by list(ENT_TYPE = "PERSON", OP = "+"), would also match, but it would run on into a second person who directly follows the first, joining “Prof. Jane Smith” and “Bob Jones” into one entity. Both titles need to be listed with and without a full stop, since the English models keep “Prof.” as one token.

txt <- "Prof. Jane Smith Bob Jones and Dr. Kim Park spoke."
spacy_initialize()
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id       text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Jane Smith   PERSON        2      2
## 2  text1  Bob Jones   PERSON        4      2
## 3  text1   Kim Park   PERSON        8      2
spacy_finalize()

spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = title_rule)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id             text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Prof. Jane Smith   PERSON        1      3
## 2  text1        Bob Jones   PERSON        4      2
## 3  text1     Dr. Kim Park   PERSON        7      3
spacy_finalize()

as_entity_patterns() checks the structure of token patterns, and converts them to the form spaCy expects: for instance, the values of IN stay a list even when there is only one. spaCy checks the attribute names and values when the rules are added, and spacy_initialize() shows its message if it does not accept them.

Rules and the model

spacyr adds its entity ruler at the end of the pipeline, after the model’s named entity recognizer and anything else that sets entities. This is what allows the title rule to build on the model’s PERSON entities.

Where a rule’s entity overlaps one that the model found, the rule’s entity is kept. With overwrite_entities = FALSE, the model’s entity is kept instead, so that the rules only add entities where the model found none:

txt <- "Jane Smith flew to Paris."
spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = c(LOC = "Paris"))
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id       text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Jane Smith   PERSON        1      2
## 2  text1      Paris      LOC        5      1
spacy_finalize()

spacy_initialize(entity_patterns = c(LOC = "Paris"), overwrite_entities = FALSE)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity(txt)
##   doc_id       text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Jane Smith   PERSON        1      2
## 2  text1      Paris      GPE        5      1
spacy_finalize()

When two rules overlap, spaCy prefers the match that spans more tokens. If they span the same number of tokens, the one that starts earlier takes priority. See spaCy’s entity ruler guide.

Set entity = FALSE to disable the model’s named entity recogniser (ner). Rules based on token attributes such as IS_TITLE still work:

name_rule <- as_entity_patterns(list(
  label = "NAME",
  pattern = list(list(IS_TITLE = TRUE), list(IS_TITLE = TRUE))
))
spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE, entity_patterns = name_rule)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_parse("We met Jane Smith there.", pos = FALSE, lemma = FALSE)
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id token entity
## 1  text1           1        1    We       
## 2  text1           1        2   met       
## 3  text1           1        3  Jane NAME_B
## 4  text1           1        4 Smith NAME_I
## 5  text1           1        5 there       
## 6  text1           1        6     .
spacy_finalize()

The title rule relies on entity annotations (ENT_TYPE and ENT_IOB) from an earlier component. With ner disabled and no other component supplying entities, spacy_initialize() warns that the title rule will not match:

spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE, entity_patterns = title_rule)
## Warning: Some patterns need entities that an earlier component found (ENT_TYPE
## or ENT_IOB), but no component before spacyr's entity ruler sets entities, so
## they will not match; use spacy_initialize(entity = TRUE)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_finalize()

A saved ruler stays in the pipeline and can supply entities even with entity = FALSE. spacyr adds its own ruler after it, using spacyr_entity_ruler or a numbered variant if that name is already in use.

Dictionaries

A quanteda dictionary becomes a set of rules labelled by its top-level keys. As in quanteda, its values match in any case, and they can have wildcards: * for any characters, and ? for one. A value with wildcards matches one token for each part separated by spaces, as quanteda matches dictionary values to tokens, so "dr * who" matches three tokens.

library("quanteda")
dict <- dictionary(list(
  ORG = c("Acme Widgets", "Globex*", "Initech, Inc."),
  PERSON = "dr * who"
), tolower = FALSE)
as_entity_patterns(dict)
## Entity patterns: 4 patterns (ORG: 3, PERSON: 1)
##   ORG     "Acme Widgets" (any case)
##   ORG     [LOWER ~ /^globex.*$/]
##   ORG     "Initech, Inc." (any case)
##   PERSON  [LOWER = dr] [LOWER ~ /^.*$/] [LOWER = who]

dictionary() lowercases its values by default, so this one is made with tolower = FALSE, to keep "Inc." as spaCy’s tokenizer expects it. Here the model’s recognizer is off, so that all the entities come from the dictionary:

spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE, entity_patterns = dict)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity("ACME WIDGETS and Globexcorp met Dr Hal Who at INITECH, Inc.")
##   doc_id          text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1  ACME WIDGETS      ORG        1      2
## 2  text1    Globexcorp      ORG        4      1
## 3  text1    Dr Hal Who   PERSON        6      3
## 4  text1 INITECH, Inc.      ORG       10      3
spacy_finalize()

With valuetype = "regex", each part of a value is a regular expression for one token. These are regular expressions in the dialect of Python, which differs from that of R in some details: for instance, Python does not support "\\p{L}" for letters. Make such a dictionary with tolower = FALSE, so that escapes such as "\\D" keep their case.

Reusing the entities found

The entities that spaCy finds in one set of texts can become rules for another, for instance to make sure that the entities found in a carefully reviewed corpus are found again, or to carry entities over to a model for another language. The output of spacy_extract_entity() keeps the text of each entity as it was, and as_entity_patterns() makes a phrase of each:

spacy_initialize()
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
found <- spacy_extract_entity(c(
  "Acme Widgets hired Jane Smith.",
  "Jane Smith moved to Ruritania."
))
spacy_finalize()
found
##   doc_id         text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1 Acme Widgets   PERSON        1      2
## 2  text1   Jane Smith   PERSON        4      2
## 3  text2   Jane Smith   PERSON        1      2
## 4  text2    Ruritania      GPE        5      1

The model took “Acme Widgets” for a person. Reviewing the entities before reusing them lets us correct that, and keep only the types we want, here people and organisations. Duplicates, such as the second “Jane Smith”, are dropped:

found$ent_type[found$text == "Acme Widgets"] <- "ORG"
found <- found[found$ent_type %in% c("PERSON", "ORG"), ]
pats <- as_entity_patterns(found)
pats
## Entity patterns: 2 patterns (ORG: 1, PERSON: 1)
##   ORG     "Acme Widgets"
##   PERSON  "Jane Smith"

spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE, entity_patterns = pats)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_extract_entity("Later, Jane Smith left Acme Widgets.")
##   doc_id         text ent_type start_id length
## 1  text1   Jane Smith   PERSON        3      2
## 2  text1 Acme Widgets      ORG        6      2
spacy_finalize()

entity_extract(), which works on the output of spacy_parse(), joins the tokens of each entity with an underscore. as_entity_patterns() converts its output too, but needs to be told the concatenator, since a token that itself contains one would be changed. spacy_extract_entity() is the better source.

Combining and saving rules

Sets of rules combine with c(), and are data.frames, with one row per rule:

all_rules <- c(title_rule, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "Acme Widgets", GPE = "Ruritania")))
all_rules
## Entity patterns: 3 patterns (PERSON: 1, ORG: 1, GPE: 1)
##   PERSON  [LOWER in (dr, dr., prof, prof., professor)] [ENT_TYPE = PERSON, ENT_IOB = B] [ENT_TYPE = PERSON, ENT_IOB = I]*
##   ORG     "Acme Widgets"
##   GPE     "Ruritania"
as.data.frame(all_rules)[, c("label", "id", "case_insensitive")]
##    label   id case_insensitive
## 1 PERSON <NA>               NA
## 2    ORG <NA>            FALSE
## 3    GPE <NA>            FALSE

entity_patterns_write() saves them in spaCy’s JSONL format, with one rule per line, which spaCy can also load on its own, and entity_patterns_read() reads them back:

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")
entity_patterns_write(all_rules, file)
cat(readLines(file), sep = "\n")
## {"label":"PERSON","pattern":[{"LOWER":{"IN":["dr","dr.","prof","prof.","professor"]}},{"ENT_TYPE":"PERSON","ENT_IOB":"B"},{"ENT_TYPE":"PERSON","ENT_IOB":"I","OP":"*"}]}
## {"label":"ORG","pattern":"Acme Widgets"}
## {"label":"GPE","pattern":"Ruritania"}
identical(entity_patterns_read(file), all_rules)
## [1] TRUE

spacyr preserves case_insensitive when writing and reading JSONL. Native spaCy ignores this field, so its default ruler matches those phrases case-sensitively.

entity_patterns_read() also reads a JSON array of rules, or a text file with one phrase per line, given a label.

Speed

On a test with 5,000 sentences, 10,000 phrases added little parsing time when all used the same case-matching setting. spacyr can also combine simple single-token regular expressions, such as dictionary globs, when they share a label, ID and token attribute. Other token patterns are checked one by one. Mixing case-sensitive and case-insensitive phrases also makes large rule sets slower, because the case-insensitive phrases are matched as token patterns.
